title: How the deck is built
body:
A tarot deck has 78 cards split into two groups: 22 Major Arcana and 56 Minor Arcana. "Arcana" means secrets, so you can think of them as the greater and lesser secrets.

The Major Arcana are numbered 0 to XXI, from The Fool to The World. They show big life themes and turning points: love, power, endings, faith, awakening. Many readers see them as a story, the Fool's journey, where each card is a lesson the Fool meets along the way.

The Minor Arcana are divided into four suits of 14 cards: Wands, Cups, Swords and Pentacles. Each suit has ten numbered cards (Ace to Ten) and four court cards (Page, Knight, Queen, King). These cards describe everyday situations, feelings, people and events.

When a reading is full of Major Arcana cards, it often points to a significant chapter in your life. When it is mostly Minor Arcana, the matter is more practical and day-to-day, and more within your hands to adjust.

This app uses the Rider–Waite–Smith deck, drawn by Pamela Colman Smith in 1909. It was the first widely used deck to give every Minor card a full illustrated scene, which is why it is such a good deck for learning: the pictures tell you the meaning.

title: The four suits and their elements
body:
Each suit is linked to one of the four classical elements, and that element colours every card in the suit.

Wands are Fire: passion, will, creativity, ambition and action. Their scenes are full of movement, sprouting staffs and warm colours.

Cups are Water: emotion, love, relationships, intuition and dreams. Look for rivers, seas and people sharing or contemplating cups.

Swords are Air: thought, communication, truth, decisions and conflict. This suit can be sharp and painful, because the mind can cut both ways, but it also brings clarity.

Pentacles are Earth: money, work, the body, home and the material world. Their scenes show gardens, craftsmanship, wealth and the slow rewards of patience.

title: What the numbers mean (Ace–Ten)
body:
The numbered cards follow a pattern you can learn once and apply to every suit. Combine the number's theme with the suit's element and you have the core of the card.

Ace: a seed, a gift, a pure new beginning. Two: choice, balance, partnership. Three: growth, collaboration, first results. Four: stability, structure, rest, sometimes standing still.

Five: disruption, challenge, loss or conflict. Six: harmony restored, generosity, moving on. Seven: assessment, perseverance, testing one's position.

Eight: movement, effort, power and skill. Nine: nearing fulfilment, the intensity of almost-there. Ten: completion, the end of a cycle, sometimes its full weight.

Try it: the Five of Cups is "challenge" plus "emotion", so emotional loss. The Eight of Pentacles is "effort" plus "material world", so diligent work and skill-building. Check the pictures and you will see exactly that.

title: The court cards (Page, Knight, Queen, King)
body:
The 16 court cards often represent people in your life, sides of your own personality, or ways of approaching a situation. Each one blends its rank with its suit's element.

Pages are students and messengers: curious, young in experience, bringing news or a fresh start. Knights are action and movement: they pursue their suit's energy, sometimes to an extreme, and their horses show their pace.

Queens are mature, inward mastery: they nurture and understand their element from within. Kings are outward mastery: they lead, decide and take responsibility for their element in the world.

So the Queen of Cups is deep emotional wisdom, while the Knight of Wands is a burst of fiery enthusiasm. When a court card appears, ask: is this someone I know, or a quality I need to bring to this situation?

title: How to read a card's imagery
body:
You don't need to memorise every meaning to read a card. Start by looking. The Rider–Waite–Smith pictures were designed to be read like a scene.

Begin with the figure: what are they doing, how do they stand or sit, and what are they wearing? Notice their gaze. A figure facing the viewer feels present and direct; a figure with their back to us invites us to share their view; facing left is often read as the past or the inner world, facing right as the future or action.

Next, look at the sky. Yellow often means optimism and clarity, blue calm and intuition, grey uncertainty or sorrow, black crisis or the unknown. Clouds suggest hidden or spiritual influences.

Then the landscape: distant mountains are goals or challenges ahead, rivers and seas are emotions, gardens are abundance, castles are security or ambition. Finally, notice the colours: red for passion and action, white for purity, blue for intuition, green for growth.

Put it together in a sentence, as if you were describing a film still. That sentence is your first reading of the card. The symbol dictionary in this app can help you go deeper.

title: How positions change a card's meaning
body:
In a spread, each position asks a question, and the card answers it. The same card can read quite differently depending on where it falls.

For example, the Eight of Swords in a "past" position might describe a time you felt trapped that you have since moved beyond. In an "obstacle" position it points to a limiting belief holding you back now. In an "advice" position it might invite you to notice that the bonds are loose and you can walk free.

Read the position's question out loud, then look at the card and answer it in plain words. This keeps your reading grounded and stops you reciting a keyword list.

Also watch how cards talk to each other. Repeated suits, many Major Arcana, or figures that seem to face toward or away from one another all add meaning to the whole story.

title: Your first reading step by step
body:
Choose a simple question, ideally an open one, such as "What do I need to know about my new job?" rather than a yes-or-no question.

Shuffle the deck in whatever way feels comfortable while holding your question in mind. When it feels right, stop and draw three cards, laying them in a row: past, present, future (or situation, challenge, advice).

Look at each card in turn. Describe what you see before reaching for a meaning: the figure, the scene, the sky and the colours. Then connect it to the position's question.

Now read the three together as a story. What changes from the first card to the last? What is the overall mood? Which card stands out most strongly to you?

Finish by writing a one-line summary and one practical step you could take. That is a complete reading.

title: Building a relationship with your deck
body:
The best way to learn tarot is to use it a little every day. A daily draw takes two minutes: in the morning, shuffle and pull one card, asking "What should I notice today?"

Look at the card and note your first impression before checking any meaning. In the evening, revisit it: where did its theme show up in your day? Over weeks, the cards start to feel like familiar characters.

Keep a tarot journal. Record the date, your question, the card or cards, what you noticed in the images and how things actually turned out. Patterns appear quickly, such as a card that keeps returning during a certain kind of week.

Treat your deck with care in whatever way feels meaningful: a cloth or box to keep it in, a moment of quiet before a reading. These small habits help you shift into a reflective frame of mind.

Be patient with yourself. Every reader starts with a few cards that make sense and many that don't. Your understanding grows each time you look closely at a picture and ask what it shows you.

title: Reading the Major Arcana as a journey
body:
The 22 Major Arcana can be read as the story of the Fool, card 0, setting out into life with nothing but trust and curiosity.

In the first stage (I–VII) the Fool meets the people and structures of the outer world: the Magician's skill, the High Priestess's intuition, the Empress and Emperor as mother and father, the Hierophant's teaching, the Lovers' choice and the Chariot's drive.

In the second stage (VIII–XIV) the journey turns inward: Strength, the Hermit's solitude, the turning Wheel, Justice, the Hanged Man's surrender, Death's transformation and Temperance's healing balance.

In the final stage (XV–XXI) the Fool faces shadow and light on a cosmic scale: the Devil and the Tower break old chains and illusions, then the Star, Moon and Sun bring hope, mystery and joy, before Judgement's awakening and the World's completion.

When you draw a Major Arcana card, ask where you might be on this journey. It helps you see a hard card as a stage to pass through rather than a final verdict.
